Right that a single JSON document has no index and no way to jump to one entry: you must parse sequentially until you reach it. But you do not have to deserialize the whole file into one in-memory object first, because streaming (event-based) parsers read it piece by piece in constant memory. Line-delimited formats such as JSON Lines (one JSON value per line) are designed to be processed one record at a time. A lookup still costs a scan of the file, which is the teacher's real point.
precise_version: A single big JSON file has no index, so finding one word means parsing through the file. Streaming parsers avoid loading it all into memory, but it is still a full scan.

The ZIP format does not require extracting everything to use one member. It has a central directory near the end whose entries record each file's local-header offset, so readers (e.g. Java JARs) seek straight to one member. The real objection is that the archive still holds many logical files, and its members may be compressed, so direct byte-offset reads of the data are not possible. A ZIP is in fact a one-file container with an index, much like the design built later.
precise_version: A zip of many folders is rejected because it is still many logical files, often compressed, so you cannot do a direct byte-offset read into the dictionary data.

Uploading a CSV to S3 and querying it with Athena is correct. But the detail (01:46:23) that Athena 'creates an index, keeping it handy along with the file' is not how Athena works. Athena is a serverless SQL engine that scans the files of a table and bills per TB scanned. You reduce the scan with compression, partitioning and columnar formats such as Parquet (Athena then reads only the needed columns), not with a per-row index on CSV. A reader could wrongly expect Athena to do cheap pointed lookups on CSV.
precise_version: With Athena you can run SQL directly over CSV files in S3. It scans the files (billed per TB scanned), and partitioning or columnar formats like Parquet cut how much it has to read.

note: Good motivation, but the dictionary design (in-memory key index plus ranged GETs of single records) is a point-lookup key-value store, while Athena is a scan-based analytics engine. The shared idea is querying plain files on S3 without a database server. Athena does not work this way internally (see L-0035).

A Lucene index is generally not a single file. It is made of one or more segments, each an independent sub-index stored as a set of files, plus a segments_N commit file. The optional compound file format collapses one segment's files into a single .cfs file, but an index with several segments still has several files.
precise_version: Lucene stores an index as one or more segments (each a set of files, optionally packed into one compound .cfs file), plus a segments_N file.

Slowness and wasted disk throughput are right. 'Sectors go bad' overstates it: reads do not wear out sectors in the normal sense. What is documented is that HDDs have a rated workload (Seagate counts lifetime reads plus writes in TB/year), and above that rate 'the reliability of the drive will begin to decline'. So constant full scans shorten drive life statistically rather than directly damaging sectors.
precise_version: Scanning 0.5 TB per request is slow, wastes disk throughput and pushes drives past their rated workload, which reduces their reliability.

note: Classroom rule of thumb. Indexing is the main tool for avoiding scans, but caching, denormalisation, better data layout and batching also speed up reads. The teacher mentions caching himself in L-0006.

About 4.3 to 4.8 letters is the average length of words in running text, where short words like 'the' and 'of' repeat. For a list of distinct words, which is what a dictionary index holds, the average is much longer. Norvig's Google Books analysis gives 4.79 letters per word token but 7.60 letters per distinct word. Dictionary headwords include many long rare words, so about 8 characters is a safer estimate. The conclusion that the index fits in RAM is unaffected.
precise_version: Average English word length is about 4.8 letters in running text, but about 7-8 letters across distinct dictionary words.

note: A 4-byte integer cannot address a 1 TB file. A signed 32-bit int goes up to 2^31-1 (about 2.1 GB), and even unsigned it stops at 2^32-1 (about 4.3 GB). 1 TB is 10^12 bytes, which needs at least 40 bits, so in practice offsets are 64-bit (8-byte) integers. With 8-byte offsets the index is still only a few MB (L-0058), so the design is unchanged; only the arithmetic changes.
precise_version: For a 1 TB file the offset must be a 64-bit (8-byte) integer, because a 4-byte integer can only address about 4 GB.

The arithmetic is right for the assumptions (170,000 x 10.3 B = 1,751,000 B, about 1.75 MB). With realistic inputs (8-byte offsets, see L-0056, and words of about 7.6 characters, see L-0055) an entry is about 7.6 + 8 + 2 = 17.6 B, so the index is about 3 MB. That is still 'peanuts' for RAM, so the conclusion holds.
precise_version: The index is roughly 170,000 x (word + 8-byte offset + 2) bytes, a few MB, which fits easily in RAM.

Wrong storage term: S3 is object storage, not block storage. AWS separates three kinds. Block storage (Amazon EBS) splits data into fixed-size blocks on a disk-like volume attached to an instance. File storage (Amazon EFS) is a shared network file system. Object storage (Amazon S3) holds whole objects with metadata, reached over HTTP by key. The choice of S3 is right, but the label would give a wrong interview answer.
precise_version: A common place reachable over the network is shared storage such as object storage (S3) or a network file system. Databases are ruled out, so the file goes on object storage like S3.

The rollback point is right. The 'short window where the file cannot be served while it uploads' does not happen on S3. Updates to a single key are atomic, and a concurrent GET returns 'either the old data or the new data, but never partial or corrupt data'. The old object keeps being served until the new PUT completes. The real same-path problems are the index/offset mismatch (L-0158) and losing the old copy for rollback when versioning is off.
precise_version: Overwriting the same S3 key is atomic (readers get the old or the new object, never a partial one). But you lose the old copy for rollback unless versioning is on, and existing indexes no longer match.

note: Correct as stated for this context.

On S3 a failed or interrupted upload does not damage the existing object. Single-key updates are atomic, so readers see the old or the new object, never a partial one. The real same-path risks are a file that uploads successfully but has corrupt content, and the stale-offset problem (L-0158). Overwriting also removes the old version needed for rollback unless versioning is enabled.

A plain text file does not carry an updated_at value in its content, as the teacher says. But S3 returns object metadata (ETag, Last-Modified) on every GetObject. A ranged GET can also be made conditional with If-Match, so the request fails with 412 Precondition Failed if the object changed. A server can therefore detect a stale index without an extra call per request. Rejecting per-request checks as polling and extra work is still a fair design choice.

Merging two sorted files is linear, O(n + m). But the alternative to sorting is not necessarily O(n^2): with a small changelog in an in-memory hash map, one pass over an unsorted file is also linear (see L-0139). O(n^2) is the cost of the naive approach that scans the whole dictionary for each changelog word.
